The paper reviews vital sustainability approaches starting with green logistics implementation as well as circular economy strategies and carbon emission reduction practices (Seuring & Müller, 2008). The investigation addresses business sector obstacles which include limitations from regulations   and   cost   management   and   supplier   relations   (Kleindorfer,   Singhal,   &   Van Wassenhove, 2005). Both Airbus and Boeing maintain their eƯorts to reduce their environmental footprint but encountering challenges with total sustainable supply chain convergence. Airbus invests in green aerospace fuel development and green aircraft formation and Boeing focuses on minimizing waste along with increasing their power eƯiciency (Airbus, 2023; Boeing, 2023). The research findings prove that aerospace supply chains need better collaborative eƯorts and modern technology together with stronger regulations to gain more sustainability success. Despite progress, a number of barriers still stand in the way of the aerospace industry's widespread implementation of Sustainable Supply Chain Management (SSCM). The aerospace industry faces three main obstacles when adopting Sustainable Supply Chain Management including sustainable material expense and disrupted supply networks and diƯiculties with sustainability integration across worldwide suppliers. The industry depends heavily on supplier cooperation because it procures multiple aircraft elements from locations with diƯerent environmental rules and regulations. The use of fossil fuels together with energy-intensive production methods in the industry creates obstacles to sustainability activities yet requires hydrogen-based aircraft and improved waste management solutions for progress. The research investigates SSCM practices in the aviation sector focusing on procedures at Airbus and Boeing. The research investigates the essential sustainable practices implemented by these corporations along with their specific hurdles that emerge during implementation. This research follows a specific organization where the theory and methods section describes the research framework then the findings and discussion evaluate Airbus and Boeing's sustainability initiatives before drawing conclusions with research possibilities in the last section followed by an overview of SSCM frameworks and aerospace industry sustainability initiatives in the literature review section. Despite advancements in technology, the implementation of sustainable supply chain management (SSCM) remains challenging due to
4 the sector's reliance on non-renewable resources, emissions-heavy logistics, and the variability in global regulations. This study aims to address the question: How can sustainable supply chain management (SSCM) be eƯectively implemented in the aerospace sector to balance economic objectives with environmental responsibility?  2. Review of Literature  SSCM has increased in importance because the aerospace industry uses extensive resources while facing environmental pressure and operational requirements. This section analyzes literature related to SSCM principles in addition to sustainability programs and the diƯiculties Airbus and Boeing are encountering.  2.1 Sustainable Supply Chain Management: Definition and Frameworks  The integration of economic social and environmental factors into supply chain operations by sustainable supply chain management (SSCM) helps minimize adverse impacts yet maintain eƯectiveness and profitability according to Carter & Rogers (2008). SSCM consists of a strategic operation alignment process whose objective is sustainability achievement according to Seuring and Müller (2008). The Triple Bottom Line (TBL) created by Elkington in 1997 establishes economic and environmental and social aspects as core elements for balancing corporate activities. A concept related to the circular economy describes how you can reduce waste and make resources more eƯicient and maintain product lifetime beyond usual cycles (Geissdoerfer et al., 2017). According to Jabbour et al. (2019) the aerospace industry uses CE principles to minimize environmental eƯects through steps such as material sourcing from sustainable sources and product recycling and remanufacturing functionalities.  2.2 Key Sustainability Strategies in the Aerospace Supply Chain 2.2.1 Green Logistics and Carbon Reduction  Green logistics works to enhance distribution and warehousing and transportation processes in order to minimize both emissions and energy usage (Srivastava, 2007). Sustainable logistics development stands essential because aviation generates substantial carbon emissions by producing 2 to 3% of worldwide CO₂ emissions (Airbus, 2023). Airbus along with Boeing operates sustainable aviation initiatives that include energy-eƯicient aircraft construction and SAF implementation as well as voluntary carbon mitigation programs (2023 Boeing report).

Airbus and   Boeing experience substantial challenges   in their operations   because   of   expensive processes and complex rules as well as disrupted supply networks. (Tang, 2006). The aerospace industry needs to scale up the production of SAF while developing standard global flight rules along with greater digital supply chain involvement to sustain long-term operations (Jabbour et al., 2019). In future, there is a need to investigate on how blockchain technology and artificial intelligence (AI) can help to improve the eƯiciency and transparency of supply network. Airbus together with Boeing and the aircraft industry need to solve these issues to boost sustainability results and comply with legal requirements while supporting worldwide carbon emission goals (ICAO, 2023). "So, the advice that changed my life, 

came from my father.



 And honestly,

 it was a very simple moment, 

but it stayed with me forever.



 I had just completed two years at Infosys 

after my degree,

 I had a stable job, a salary, 

everything was comfortable. 



But I had this thought in the back of my mind, 

about going to Germany, doing my Master's, 

starting something completely new. 



And honestly, I was very scared. 

Leaving a secure job, new country, new language, 

I didn't know anyone there. 



And I kept thinking, what if…I am not good enough, 

what if I make the wrong decision. 



And my father, he just sat with me one evening, 

and he said, 

son, take the chance. 

Because if you don't, you will never know. 



And that was it. Nothing more, nothing less. 



I left Infosys, I came to Germany, 

I did my Master's, 

I got into Rolls-Royce, and honestly,



 I am sitting here today because of that one conversation. 



And what I take from that into my work every day 

is very simple.



 Don't wait for the perfect moment, 

because honestly, that moment never comes.



 You just take the chance, 

and you figure it out on the way."

"So, this is something 

I have genuinely reflected on, 

not just for interviews. 



My honest answer is,

 I have a tendency to over-analyse before I act. 



And look, 

in a safety-critical environment like Rolls-Royce, 

that instinct has real value.



 But I have learned, 

sometimes the hard way, 

that a structured 80 percent answer delivered on time, 

is more valuable than a perfect answer 

that arrives too late. 



There was a moment at Rolls-Royce, 

where I held a FRACAS escalation a little too long,

 waiting for more certainty in the data. 



My senior colleague flagged it before I did.



 Nothing went wrong, 

but the lesson was very clear. 



The data will never be perfectly complete, 

at some point you have to make the call

 with what you have.





So what I actively do now, 

is set myself clear decision points before

 I start any analysis, 

and I timebox my thinking to that. 



I still go deep, but 

I know when to stop 

and move.

 And honestly, 

that self awareness, around 

when to act versus when to keep digging,

 is something I am already much better 

at than I was two years ago."

Integrated Supply Chain Planning For Sustainable Urban Mobility: A Case Analysis Of Greenmotion Mobility Solutions  March 10, 2026  Report By: Sanket Agalave (242951) Guide- Dr. Behrooz Gharleghi Department of Strategic Management in Logistics BBW Hochschule, Berlin, Germany  Abstract.   The rapid growth of sustainable urban mobility has increased the importance of efficient and integrated supply chain planning for companies operating in the electric mobility sector. This study analyzes the supply chain planning structure of GreenMotion Mobility Solutions (GMS), a European manufacturer of electric bicycles and light electric mobility devices. The company operates a globally distributed supply chain involving component sourcing from Asia and Eastern Europe, assembly operations in Central Europe, and distribution across multiple European markets. The paper examines the structure of GMS’s supply chain, identifies key planning challenges related to demand volatility, global sourcing, and distribution complexity, and evaluates the organizational planning structure currently in place. In addition, the study explores how sustainability considerations are reflected in supply chain decisions and analyzes key trade-offs between cost, service level, and environmental   performance.   Managerial   optimization   approaches   are   discussed   to   improve coordination in distribution and replenishment planning. Finally, the paper develops potential future scenarios that could affect GMS’s supply chain, including disruptions in component sourcing and demand surges resulting from European mobility policies. The findings highlight the importance of integrated supply chain planning to improve operational efficiency, sustainability, and supply chain resilience.

Introduction  The demand for electric bicycles and other light electric mobility devices has dramatically expanded throughout Europe due to the quick development of sustainable urban mobility solutions. Supply Chain Structure and Global Footprint  In order to facilitate the manufacture and distribution of electric bicycles and other light electric mobility devices throughout European markets, GreenMotion Mobility Solutions (GMS) runs a worldwide supply chain network. By combining regional production, worldwide sourcing, and multi-country distribution operations, the firm is able to strike a balance between cost effectiveness and market responsiveness. The case description states that GMS gets parts from across the world, assembles them in Central Europe, and distributes completed goods through a number of distribution facilities that cater to clients in various EU member states. In order to increase efficiency and service standards, several supply chain stages are regionally optimized in this arrangement, which is representative of a typical global supply chain structure.  2.1 Global Supply Chain Configuration  GreenMotion Mobility Solutions runs a globally distributed supply chain that combines regional distribution, European production, and global sourcing. With this arrangement, the business

Key Planning Challenges  Global component procurement, European manufacture, and distribution across many EU countries are all part of the intricate global supply chain in which GreenMotion Mobility Solutions (GMS) works. The corporation can reach a large consumer base thanks to this network, but it also presents a number of planning issues. Aligning supply and demand throughout the company is particularly challenging due to demand volatility, worldwide sourcing relationships, and the complexity of the distribution   network.   Planning   choices   within   GMS   are   now   dispersed   across   procurement, production, and logistics units, as detailed in the case background, which makes coordination even more difficult.  3.1 Demand Volatility  Demand   volatility   is   one of   the main   planning   issues GMS faces.   Seasonal   patterns, government incentives for environmentally friendly transportation, and shifting customer tastes can all affect the demand for electric bicycles. These differences might result in mismatches between production and market demand and complicate demand forecasting. Distribution facilities may have surplus stock or inventory shortages as a result of inaccurate projections. Additionally, the bullwhip effect—in which minor changes in consumer demand result in greater variances in orders and production levels across the supply chain—may be brought on by demand variability (Chopra & Meindl, 2019).  3.2 Global Sourcing Risks  Additional difficulties with lead periods for shipping and supply interruptions are brought about by global sourcing. Shipments must travel great distances before arriving at assembly sites in Europe   because   essential   components   are   acquired   from   Asian   vendors. The supply of essential components may be disrupted by events like port congestion, shipping delays, or geopolitical instability. The availability of completed goods in European markets may be impacted by production activities' potential delays.  3.3 Distribution Complexity  Supply chain complexity is also increased by managing distribution across several European nations. In order to adapt to different regional demand patterns, GMS must effectively distribute   inventory   among   many   distribution   sites.   Distribution   centers   may   encounter inventory imbalances in the absence of integrated planning procedures, which might have a detrimental impact on service quality and operational effectiveness.
5  3.4 Importance of Integrated Supply Chain Planning  Implementing integrated supply chain planning becomes crucial for GMS in its present growth stage in light of these obstacles. Coordinating demand forecasts, procurement, production scheduling, and distribution choices throughout the whole supply chain is known as integrated planning. Integrated planning unifies all supply chain operations around a common demand forecast and shared performance goals, as opposed to functioning in functional silos (Stadtler, 2015). Integrated planning may provide GMS a number of significant advantages, including: 1. Better supply and demand alignment, which lowers the possibility of stockouts and surplus inventories. 2. Improved departmental collaboration, encompassing sales, manufacturing, logistics, and procurement. 3. Improved supply chain insight allows for quicker reactions to interruptions or shifts in demand. 4. More efficient sustainability planning that enables sourcing and transportation decisions to take emissions into account. Organizations may synchronize strategic, tactical, and operational decisions throughout the supply chain by using integrated planning frameworks like Sales and Operations Planning (S&OP)   or   Integrated   Business   Planning   (IBP).   GMS   may   enhance   supply   chain responsiveness, lower operational inefficiencies, and promote sustainable growth in the quickly growing electric mobility sector by putting such procedures into place.  4. Organizational Structure and Planning Coordination  Coordination between various organizational units in charge of procurement, manufacturing, sales, logistics, and sustainability is necessary for effective supply chain planning. S&OP is a popular paradigm for supply chain planning that uses an organized cross-functional planning process to coordinate choices   on   distribution,   procurement,   production   scheduling,   and   demand   forecasting (Stadtler,2015). Implementing S&OP would improve the organization's vertical and horizontal integration.  Horizontal Integration  Improved coordination across several functional departments at the same organizational level is referred to as horizontal integration. Representatives from the departments of sales, procurement, manufacturing, logistics, and sustainability would work together to create a single, consensus-based demand and supply plan through frequent S&OP meetings. Benefits of horizontal integration include:     Improved alignment between demand forecasts and production capacity.     Better coordination between procurement and manufacturing schedules.     More efficient distribution and replenishment planning across warehouses.  Vertical Integration  Aligning strategic, tactical, and operational planning choices across several managerial levels is known as vertical integration. Top management may connect long-term strategic objectives, such market development plans and sustainability targets, with operational supply chain choices by using an S&OP framework. Key benefits include:     Stronger alignment between corporate strategy and supply chain operations.     Improved decision-making based on shared performance metrics.     Enhanced ability to respond to supply chain disruptions and demand changes. By implementing an integrated S&OP process, GMS can transition from a fragmented planning structure toward a more coordinated and responsive supply chain management approach.

Conclusion  This report examined the supply chain planning structure of GreenMotion Mobility Solutions (GMS) and evaluated the challenges and opportunities associated with managing a globally distributed supply chain. The analysis showed that the company operates a complex network involving global component sourcing, European assembly operations, and regional distribution centers serving multiple European markets. While this structure enables cost efficiency and broad market access, it also introduces planning challenges related to demand volatility, global sourcing risks, and distribution complexity. The study identified that the current planning structure within GMS is largely decentralized, with procurement,   production,   and   logistics   functions   operating   in   separate   planning   silos.   This fragmentation reduces coordination across the supply chain and makes it more difficult to align demand forecasts, production schedules, and distribution decisions. Implementing an integrated planning framework such as Sales and Operations Planning (S&OP) would improve collaboration across departments and enhance both horizontal and vertical integration. Abstract:   The fast-evolving nature of the market of intralogistics of present days requires strategic   purchasing   and   supplier   management (PSM)   as the means of maintaining   a competitive edge, especially in tech-driven companies, such as SSI Schafer. To cut costs, reduce the risk, and promote sustainability, the present work has examined the means by which SSI Schafer can enhance its procurement activities. The paper explains the problems of the company and proposes a Supplier strategy based on the dynamic requirements and ecosystem of secondary data, procurement KPIs and supplier analysis models like the Kraljic Matrix. The findings highlight the need to have sustainable sourcing practices, digital tracking of performance, and co-invention. The proposed plan is to ensure SSI Schafer supply chain survivability and sustainability in market domination.  Keywords:   Strategic   Purchasing,   Supplier   Management,   SSI   Schäfer,   Intralogistics, Procurement KPIs, Sustainability, Kraljic Matrix, Digital Procurement, Supply Chain Resilience  I. Introduction:  In the context of automation, digitalization, and global turbulence, the ability to respond to fluctuations in the supply chain has entered the profile of strategic conditions as a priority of production and logistic companies. PSM and strategic buying is now considered   a   front-office   process   not   a   back-office   process,   since   at   most organizations   it   plays   a   pivotal   role   in   enabling   sustainability,   innovation,   and competitive differentiation. The procurement excellence is essential to SSI Schafer, a global leader in warehouse automation and intralogistics, to maintain position in the market and to fulfil its mission, called Think Tomorrow. Having its headquarters in Neunkirchen in Germany with more than 70 countries of operation, SSI SchAfer was established in 1937 and serves in many industries, some of   which   include   retail,   food   and   beverage,   pharmaceuticals,   e-commerce   and automotive   industry.   The   firm   sells   intelligent   storage   systems,   robotics,   work equipment, automated guided vehicles (AGV) and conveyor technology and logistic software such as warehouse management systems (WMS). With so many advanced and modular options to choose, the task of procurement is key to acquiring high tech, high standards of components, fulfilling the specific needs of high demands of operation. The   task   before   SSI   Schafer   in   this   respect   is   to   provide   harmony   between sustainability,   risk   management,   as   well   as   cost   control.   The   growing   level   of uncertainty in the supply networks is not properly addressed using conventional cost- based approaches. In the meantime, consumers are driving increased pressure through their rising volume of demands of traceability, low-carbon products, and fast customisation on upstream procurement systems. Due to this, the company SSI Sch really considers strategic supplier management not just as an operational problem, but rather a component of its growth and innovation objective. To enhance loads of productivity, minimize risks and achieve long-terms goals in sustainability, this research paper explores the way SSI SchAfer could enhance its purchasing processes. The analysis based on the theoretical frameworks, performance indicators of procurement and industry standards proposes the course of future action in studying the current situation. This research paper will help the company of SSI Schafer to enhance its ability to deal with complexity, to embark more on supplier collaboration in the promotion of innovation and to continue its leadership in the highly competitive intralogistics market by understanding better PSM.
II. Research Question and Research Problem: A. Research Question:  The challenging and very competitive intralogistic market that SSI Schafer is based in demands absolute performance and sustainability fetishes in its supply chains as its supply chains grow progressively international as well as virtual. The company offers a complete variety of complex inputs including mass standardized steel to support racking systems, advanced robots, and AI- intelligent software. This volatility poses major challenges to the supplier and purchase   management,   though   it   fosters   creativeness   and   flexibility   of products. The fact that SSI Schafer is struggling to balance between the three major goals of procurement namely ensuring that procurement has been sustainable, that it minimizes risk, and that it is cost-effective is one of the greatest challenges that this store is currently experiencing. The enterprises are under pressure in terms of cost due to global competition; therefore, it has to cut costs in terms of input repeatedly without compromising quality. It also has to deal with increasing supply risks, including reliance on specialty or   legacy   vendors   to   provide   custom   parts,   raw   material   scarcity   and disruptions due to geopolitical turmoil. Besides, the growing importance of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) criteria makes the process of selecting and monitoring suppliers more challenging. This is a multidimensional issue that seems to urgently need to be addressed by the company: how to make procurement solutions and practices more sustainable and keep the operations efficient.  2. Research Problem:  Given these challenges, this study seeks to answer the following core research question:  “How can SSI Schäfer improve its purchasing and supplier management strategy to reduce risks, lower costs, and support sustainable growth?”  The following question defines the analysis framework of the paper and assesses   the   current   system   used   by   SSI   Scharfer   and   provides recommendations in terms of strategic steps that will support the goals of resilience, innovation, and sustainability.  III. Data Collection  Because it utilizes already available sources in order to understand the plans of suppliers of SSI Schafer, its performance indicators and procurement processes, this research   report   assumes   RSD   gathering.   The   fact   that   it   has   access   to   a comprehensive scope of information including internal corporate documents, industry standards,   or   even   academic   research   systems   on   topics   related   to   strategic purchasing   and   supplier   managements makes the   utilization   of   secondary   data suitable in this research.

Research Overview  In this section, the key modules of the SSI Schafer purchasing system are outlined, as well as a structural understanding of the supplier segmentation methods, purchasing classification, and the procurement model of the company in general. Before providing a more detailed study, the aim is to put data into perspective.  A. Overview of Purchased Items and Services  At SSI Schafer due to the location at the border between mechanical engineering, electronics and digital logistics, the procurement operation encompasses a large diversification in the materials, components and services. The principal types of the purchased products are as follows, along with the accordingly assigned percentage of the total volume of the procurements:  1. controllers (PLCs), wiring, and sensors to be of the utmost importance, which is why they could be defined as strategic. 3. Other Materials and Technologies (7%)  This encompasses advanced technology such as artificial intelligence (AI) equipment, environment friendly resources and next generation materials that are being worked on today. Such combination of very specific and uniform components requires a specialised purchasing strategy supported through strategic alignment and an effective supplier segmentation.  B. Supplier Segmentation Using the Kraljic Matrix  SSI Schafer utilizes the Kraljic Portfolio Matrix in order to organize the purchased items into two categories based on the two factors: profit effect and supply risk.  Strategic Items (High Risk / High Profit Impact)  It also incorporates licensed WMS software, advanced control systems and precision robotic parts most of the above must share risk arrangements and close work, plus develop together.     Leverage Items (Low Risk / High Profit Impact)  This category consists of plastic resins and high volume steel parts. It is imperative to be cost effective, which could be implemented by establishing long term framework agreements, introduction of competitive bidding and application of volume bundling.     Bottleneck Items (High Risk / Low Profit Impact)  Specialized consulting services, customized spare parts and legacy chips are difficult to get. SSI Schäfer lessens such a risk by researching alternative design and maintaining safety stocks.     Non-Critical Items (Low Risk / Low Profit Impact)  With minimal monitoring, this type of office equipment, fasteners, and MRO consumables are managed using transactional or catalog based procurement systems.  C.    Global Efficiency : Centralized contracts also ensure that there are superior price and technological partnerships to strategic or high-volume elements.     Local Responsiveness : Shorter lead time and regional logistical, customer and regulatory coordination are made possible by regional buying units.  V. Data Analysis  By utilizing the KPIs and evaluating criteria of procurement as well as adapting technologies, this section will evaluate the effectiveness and output of SSI Schafer supplier management and purchasing processes. This is done in order to assess the extent to which the procurement system of the organization meets strategic objectives in terms of cost, quality, delivery of services, risk and sustainability.  A. Supplier Selection Criteria  The SSI Schafer employs a systematic approach when selecting the suppliers viewing at both qualitative and quantitative aspects. These are some of the principal factors:     Technical Capability   Suppliers should demonstrate contemporary production talents particularly in the automation and robotics technology.     Product Quality : Strict following of specification and low rate of failure is the basis of reliability and safety of warehouse installations     Cost Competitiveness : Even when total cost of ownership (TCO) is considered, pricing is a large issue especially among leverage items.     Delivery Reliability : OTD is crucial to meeting the project deadlines and avoiding costly project delays.     Innovation Potential : Preference is given to suppliers, which support modular, scalable design, and co-development Supplier.     Proximity and Flexibility : The suppliers are given preference like nearshore suppliers, EU-based suppliers, to decrease geopolitical risk and lead times. Digital and Sustainable Procurement Tools  By progressively implementing Kodiak Hub and other Supplier Performance Management (SPM) system, the SSI Schafer Company plans to resolve the problem of the lack of data visibility and decision-making. These solutions have real-time dashboards where cross- functional visibility can be achieved, any abnormalities in performance can be discovered and data regarding KPI made to aggregate.
VI. Findings:  As the international supply chain incurs delays, customer demands have shifted, and environmental concerns have advanced, SSI Schafer has been forcefully enhancing its procurement and supplier management methods based on an examination of the procurement system of the company. However, the number of operation and strategic hurdles remains.  A. Key Procurement Challenges  a)   Supply Chain Risk Exposure  Highly precise sensors, software modules, and sophisticated robotic parts, many of which are in the Strategic and Bottleneck categories of the Kraljic Matrix, are mostly sourced by SSI Schafer with the help of specialist vendors. This concentration lends greater vulnerability to the supply chain, especially in cases whereby the alternate technology or alternate sources are limited. b) Quality and Performance Variability Even when the rates of on-time delivery have been improving, the rates of defect rates are still an issue, as they are 35 in 2021 and 88 in 2024. A mix of supplier output of 700 PPM on average in 2024 is translated into instability within the supplier output, which can potentially influence the reliability of the company processes itself and project schedules. c) ESG Compliance and Sustainability Integration It means that SSI Schafer is also on the way to realizing traditional methods of procurement and moving toward a more ethical and sustainable system, as by 2024 only 30% of suppliers will have obtained an ESG mark. This region requires urgent scaled up because the customer expectations and regulatory guidelines can only be strong globally such as the EU Corporate Sustainability reporting Directive (CSRD).  B. Strategic Procurement Strengths a) Hybrid Global-Local Sourcing Model  By using regional procurement centers to ensure responsiveness, SSI Schäfer's hybrid buying strategy enables it to take advantage of centralized contracts for essential components. Without sacrificing cost-effectiveness, this dual strategy improves operational flexibility.  b) Structured Supplier Evaluation System  The company has established an effective supplier performance management system that focuses on quality performance indicators such as OTD, the rate of defects, communication, and sustainability. The measurements provide a good foundation of strategic decision- making and compliments with the best practice of supplier performance management.  c) Move Toward Co-Innovation  The approach of integrating key suppliers, especially in the area of robotics and digital systems as well as through collaborative research and development and long-term collaboration indicates an upcoming form of co-innovation that is future ready. This
encourages better customisation, faster integration of technology and value generation mutuality.  d) Internal Procurement Optimization  The desire to standardize procurement operations across SSI SchAfer subsidiaries with the help of SLAs and associated KPIs can be regarded as one of the clear steps toward internal efficiency and strategy alignment. This assists in the provision of better internal services, planning, and forecasting.  C. Strategic Implications     Failure to accelerate its digital and ESG transition will leave SSI Schafer at risk of falling behind the marketplace leaders that have fully incorporated sustainability and real-time analyticsologies in their procurement processes.     The concentration of the company suppliers on such high-risk categories as to reduce potential incoming disruptions, it is called to further diversify and implement multi-sourcing.     Cultivation of talent in the domain of procurement is important to the operationalization the proposed ecosystem strategy especially the ones related to analytics, negotiation, and ESG sourcing.
VII. Conclusions  Under this study, SSI Schafer is progressing slowly toward the modernized procurement strategy yet the company has to speed up its transition to address the future challenges. The business has to deal with quality, cost, risk and sustainability in a highly diversified and technologically straining supply chain in a strategic and constructive manner. The following strategic actions are recommended: 1.   Accelerate Digital Integration  Real-time supplier tracking should eliminate barriers to responsiveness and attainability: boost real-time tracking to over 85% by 2027. 2.   Strengthen ESG Compliance  Restrict the percentage of the suppliers rated in accordance with ESG to 85%, so that the procurement would be in full compliance with the legal and sustainability requirements. 3.   Enhance Risk Management  To reduce dependence on supply interruption, high-risk components should be worked on using dual- or multi-sourcing approaches. 4.   Foster Co-Innovation  Innovate and customise more, consolidate R&D partnership with key suppliers, most notably in robotics and digital systems. 5.   Develop Procurement Talent  In an attempt to support the pursuit of these goals, train internal value teams on strategic negotiation, analytics and ESG sourcing..  The concepts of resilience, digital intelligence, and sustainability can be incorporated into supplier relationships of SSI Schafer in order to transition the process of procurement into a strategic value-creation process instead of a cost center. This change will be required to sustain the desire of the company to think tomorrow and to remain the global leader in the sphere of intralogistics. .

"Inventory Insights: Data-Driven Improvement Techniques for Metro Ag's Supply Chain"  JUNE 26, 2025  Project By – Agalave, Sanket (242951) Guide – Prof. Vadim Ermakov Department of Strategic Management in Logistics BBW Hochschule, Berlin, Germany
Abstract:   Inventory management plays a vital role in ensuring supply chain eƯiciency, especially for wholesale enterprises managing diverse product categories. This research investigates how Metro AG, a global wholesaler operating in both perishable and non- perishable   segments,   can   enhance   its   inventory   operations   through   data-driven methods. The study identifies key inventory challenges such as stock imbalances, SKU complexity, and ineƯiciencies in ordering practices. By leveraging techniques like ABC analysis, Economic Order Quantity (EOQ), and demand forecasting, the research proposes a structured framework to optimize Metro AG's stock management. Data was collected from secondary sources including industry reports, academic literature, and publicly available data from Metro AG. Through qualitative case study analysis and comparative   insights,   the   findings   reveal   that   implementing   structured   inventory classification and predictive models can significantly reduce costs, minimize waste, and improve service levels. This research aims to oƯer practical solutions not only for Metro AG but also for similar wholesale SMEs navigating complex inventory environments.  Keywords:   Inventory management, Metro AG, ABC analysis, Economic Order Quantity (EOQ),   demand   forecasting,   supply   chain   optimization,   wholesale   logistics,   SME operations  I.   Introduction  Inventory management is a foundational pillar of supply chain success, particularly in sectors dealing with high product variety and dynamic demand, such as wholesale and retail. For companies like Metro AG—one of the largest global   wholesalers   with   operations   spanning   both   food   and   non-food categories—managing inventory eƯectively is not just a logistical necessity but a strategic imperative. Metro AG handles thousands of Stock Keeping Units (SKUs), ranging from perishable food products requiring cold-chain logistics to long-shelf-life   non-food   items.   This   operational   complexity   introduces challenges in maintaining optimal stock levels, preventing stockouts, and minimizing holding costs. In today's competitive and unpredictable business landscape, the cost of inventory mismanagement is high. Overordering leads to increased storage and waste, especially with perishable goods, while underordering results in lost sales, reduced customer satisfaction, and disrupted supply chains. Traditional methods such as periodic reviews or static reordering points often fail to adapt to real-time market conditions or seasonality in demand. Amid these challenges, data-driven inventory techniques like ABC analysis, Economic Order Quantity (EOQ), and demand forecasting oƯer significant opportunities for improvement. These methods enable businesses to segment inventory based on value and demand patterns, calculate optimal order
quantities, and anticipate future needs with greater accuracy. However, despite their proven benefits, many SMEs—including Metro AG—struggle with inconsistent   implementation   due   to   fragmented   data   systems,   limited predictive capabilities, and manual practices in certain regions. This research aims to explore how Metro AG can overcome these inventory management hurdles by implementing structured and analytical techniques. Through secondary data analysis and a case study approach, the study provides insights into how Metro AG can reduce waste, cut costs, and enhance service levels using modern inventory methods. The outcomes are intended to oƯer practical recommendations for Metro AG and similar SMEs operating in complex supply chain environments.  II.   Research Questions and Research Problem: Research Problem  Despite   advances   in   supply   chain   technologies,   many   businesses— particularly large-scale Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) like Metro AG— continue to face persistent inventory management challenges. The company operates across a wide product range that includes perishable and non- perishable   goods,   which   significantly   increases   complexity   in   inventory classification, stock planning, and order fulfillment. Metro AG’s current practices often rely on historical sales data, manual or partially automated systems, and periodic review cycles. These methods, while functional, lack the adaptability required for real-time responsiveness and eƯiciency. As a result, Metro AG experiences   common inventory issues such as overstocking,   understocking,   high   holding   costs,   and   demand unpredictability—especially   for   seasonal   and   fast-moving   goods.   These ineƯiciencies   lead   to   increased   operational   expenses   and   diminished customer satisfaction. Furthermore, the absence of systematic product categorization   (e.g.,   ABC   analysis)   and   limited   application   of   cost- optimization models like EOQ results in the equal treatment of high- and low- priority items. Without leveraging modern analytical tools, Metro AG is at risk of failing to meet customer demand eƯiciently while incurring excessive costs. Given the strategic importance of inventory optimization in wholesale supply chains, there is a pressing need to evaluate Metro AG’s current practices and explore more eƯicient, data-driven solutions.  Research Question  What are the key inventory challenges faced by Metro AG, and how can techniques such as ABC analysis, Economic Order Quantity (EOQ), and demand forecasting improve the eƯiciency, accuracy, and cost-eƯectiveness of its inventory management system?
III.   Data Collection:  This research utilizes a secondary data collection approach to explore Metro AG’s inventory challenges and evaluate the potential improvements oƯered by analytical techniques like ABC analysis, EOQ, and demand forecasting. Secondary data was chosen due to the availability of reliable academic literature, industry case studies, and Metro AG's publicly accessible business reports and catalogs.  Sources of Secondary Data  The following types of data were used to build the foundation of this research:  A.   Academic Literature and Research Articles  Peer-reviewed journals and textbooks provided in-depth insights into inventory management strategies, including the theory and application of ABC analysis, EOQ models, safety stock optimization, and demand forecasting techniques. Justification for Method  Using secondary data allowed for a comprehensive and cost-eƯective exploration of Metro AG’s supply chain without the need for time-intensive fieldwork or internal company data access. This method also enabled triangulation across various credible sources to ensure accuracy and relevancy of insights.
IV.   Research Overview:  This research centers on the operational and strategic importance of inventory optimization for Metro AG, a global wholesale company dealing with complex supply chains. The study builds on the premise that traditional inventory approaches—relying on static reordering points and retrospective sales data—are no longer suƯicient in today’s dynamic retail and wholesale environment. In particular, Metro AG, with its large and varied assortment of both perishable and non-perishable goods, faces unique challenges in aligning demand with supply, minimizing inventory costs, and maintaining service quality.  Relevance of the Topic  Inventory management has gained new relevance due to global supply chain disruptions, inflationary pressures, and shifting customer expectations. The ability to respond quickly and accurately to demand changes is essential for maintaining competitiveness, especially in the food wholesale sector where product freshness and shelf-life constraints play a critical role. SMEs like Metro AG must now seek data-driven approaches that balance operational eƯiciency with financial prudence.  Research Objectives  The main objectives of this study are: 1.   To identify key inventory management challenges faced by Metro AG, particularly in handling a wide variety of SKUs with diƯering demand patterns and perishability. 2.   To analyze Metro AG’s current inventory methods such as periodic reviews, stock-level triggers, and historical sales-based reordering. 3.   To apply and evaluate data-driven techniques—ABC analysis, Economic Order Quantity (EOQ), and demand forecasting—for improving inventory accuracy and cost eƯiciency. 4.   To propose actionable strategies that can enhance Metro AG’s inventory operations and serve as a model for similar SMEs in the wholesale industry.  Research Structure  The research follows a phased approach:     Phase I: Identifying inventory challenges at Metro AG     Phase II: Reviewing current inventory practices     Phase III: Applying proposed techniques (ABC, EOQ)     Phase IV: Drawing comparisons, making observations, and concluding with recommended improvements This structured approach ensures that the analysis is both holistic and practical, enabling the transition from theoretical models to real-world application within Metro AG’s operational context.
V.   Data Analysis:  This section provides an in-depth analysis of Metro AG’s inventory practices using   established   inventory   management   techniques:   ABC   Analysis, Economic Order Quantity (EOQ), and a qualitative overview of demand forecasting practices. The analysis is based on the data collected from secondary sources, including Metro AG’s product documentation and case examples, and academic literature on inventory models.  A. Current Inventory Practices at Metro AG  Based on public company data and case references, Metro AG currently employs a mix of basic inventory control methods, including:     Periodic   inventory   reviews   with   safety   stock   to   buƯer   against uncertainties. While eƯective for avoiding stockouts, this often leads to overstocking and high holding costs.     Stock-level triggers   for reordering, using minimum stock thresholds. However, these are largely static and not dynamically updated with real- time demand changes.     Manual or semi-automated systems   in certain regions, which leads to inconsistent implementation and fragmented data handling.     Limited use of item-level classification , resulting in equal treatment of critical and non-critical items in procurement and stocking decisions. These practices highlight an overreliance on historical data and a lack of segmentation   in   inventory   control,   which   impairs   agility   and   cost- eƯectiveness.  B. ABC Analysis: Inventory Segmentation ABC analysis   is a method of categorizing inventory based on its importance— usually measured by consumption value. Applying this to Metro AG's product range (e.g., perishable goods like beef tenderloin, salmon fillets, and olive oil), we observe:     Category A Items : High-value products, typically contributing to 70–80% of total inventory value but representing only 10–15% of SKUs. These items require close monitoring and frequent reviews.     Category B Items : Medium-priority products with moderate consumption and value.     Category C Items : Low-value items that form the majority of SKUs but contribute minimally to inventory value.

C. EOQ: Optimizing Order Size  The   Economic Order Quantity (EOQ)   model calculates the ideal order quantity that minimizes total inventory costs (ordering + holding). For Metro AG’s salmon fillet, the following parameters were used:     Annual Demand (D):   12,000 units (1,000/month)     Ordering Cost (S):   €60 per order (admin and logistics)     Holding Cost (H):   €4 per unit/year (storage, freezing)  Interpretation : Metro AG should order   600 units   of this product per replenishment cycle. This reduces both the number of orders placed and the average inventory held, ultimately lowering overall costs. Tables For the Yearly EOQ Analysis:

Demand Forecasting: Anticipating Needs  Although Metro AG currently relies on historical data,   demand forecasting  models such as time-series analysis or moving averages can improve order planning—especially for seasonal goods. These models help anticipate fluctuations in demand, allowing dynamic adjustment of safety stock levels and reducing the risk of stockouts or overstocking.  Recommendation : Implement basic forecasting tools (e.g., Excel-based moving average) for products with strong seasonality or frequent turnover.  VI.   Findings  The application of data-driven inventory management techniques revealed several actionable insights that can enhance Metro AG’s supply chain eƯiciency. Through the lens of ABC analysis, EOQ modeling, and demand forecasting, this research identified key gaps in current practices and validated the benefits of adopting structured analytical approaches.  A. Improved Inventory Prioritization through ABC Analysis  ABC analysis enabled a clear segmentation of Metro AG's vast product range based on consumption value and criticality. By identifying high-value, fast-
moving items such as beef tenderloin and Atlantic salmon fillets as Category A items, Metro AG can:     Allocate more resources and tighter control to these critical SKUs.     Reduce the risk of stockouts for top-selling products.     Avoid over-investment in low-impact items. This segmentation also supports better purchasing decisions and warehouse space planning by shifting focus to items that have the greatest impact on revenue and customer satisfaction.  B. Cost Optimization through EOQ  The EOQ model demonstrated its value in balancing ordering and holding costs. In the case of the Atlantic salmon fillet:     The calculated EOQ of 600 units per order resulted in fewer orders per year, reducing administrative and transport-related overhead.     Holding cost optimization led to more eƯicient use of cold storage facilities, which is particularly relevant for perishable inventory.     The model promoted leaner inventory practices by aligning order size with actual annual demand and cost structures. This approach stands in stark contrast to Metro AG’s existing practice of bulk ordering without optimization, which risks both overstocking and increased waste.  C. Predictive Capability through Demand Forecasting  Although the forecasting models were not deeply embedded in Metro AG’s current operations, the study highlights the value of even simple forecasting techniques, such as:     Moving averages for regularly selling items.     Trend analysis for products with known seasonality.     Safety stock calibration based on forecast variability.
Such techniques can drastically reduce the mismatch between inventory levels and real-time demand, especially for seasonal goods and promotional stock-keeping units.  D. Organizational Benefits  If implemented correctly, these techniques can help Metro AG achieve:     Inventory cost reductions   (ordering, holding, spoilage)     Improved product availability   for top-tier items     Reduced waste , especially in perishable goods     Enhanced customer satisfaction   through fewer stockouts     More accurate procurement planning   and vendor coordination These findings suggest a strong business case for modernizing Metro AG’s inventory systems using data-driven tools.  VII.   Conclusions  EƯicient inventory management is critical for the profitability and service quality of wholesale companies like Metro AG, especially when handling a vast and diverse product portfolio. This research set out to address the key inventory challenges faced by Metro AG and explore how analytical tools such as ABC analysis, Economic Order Quantity (EOQ), and demand forecasting can improve its inventory operations.  The findings demonstrate that Metro AG’s current reliance on historical data, manual   reviews,   and   static   reordering   strategies   contributes   to   stock imbalances, excess holding costs, and ineƯiciencies in meeting customer demand. In contrast, a structured and data-driven approach can segment inventory by value and demand, reduce ordering frequency, optimize stock levels, and better align supply with real-time consumption patterns. ABC analysis enables Metro AG to prioritize critical items, thereby improving availability for high-demand products and reducing working capital lock-in. EOQ helps the company strike a balance between ordering and holding costs, minimizing logistical waste. Demand forecasting, even when applied at a basic level, oƯers significant advantages   in anticipating seasonal   trends and optimizing replenishment cycles. Adopting these methods requires more than just technical tools—it also calls for process alignment, improved data integration across regions, and staƯ training. However, the long-term benefits in terms of cost reduction, enhanced agility, and customer satisfaction make a compelling case for implementation. This research contributes practical insights not only for Metro AG but also for other SMEs in the wholesale and retail sector striving to improve supply chain eƯiciency. Future studies could expand by incorporating real-time data, machine learning models, or pilot implementation feedback to evaluate the operational impact of such techniques more deeply.

Abstract:  This paper explores logistics network planning in the context of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), with a focus on LPG BioMarkt GmbH as a case study. While much of the literature focuses on large-scale, global logistics networks, SMEs often face resource limitations that require simpler yet effective approaches. In order to balance cost-effectiveness and delivery responsiveness, this study looks at how SMEs might optimize logistics networks utilizing simple tools, zone clustering, and cooperative tactics.  Keywords:   SME logistics, regional distribution, LPG BioMarkt, cost- responsiveness tradeoff, zone clustering, collaborative distribution  I.   Introduction  Logistics plays a vital role in ensuring the competitiveness and sustainability   of   small-scale   manufacturers,   particularly   those operating within regional markets. Efficient logistics networks help businesses reduce operational costs, enhance customer satisfaction, and respond effectively to market demand. However, the majority of existing logistics research and frameworks are developed with large-scale, global corporations in mind, leaving a gap in guidance for SMEs with limited resources and simpler operational scopes. In the context of small enterprises, logistics decisions are often constrained   by   financial   limitations,   reduced   access   to technology, and smaller delivery volumes. Yet, SMEs must still meet customer expectations for responsiveness, reliability, and transparency. Therefore, maintaining long-term survival requires finding the ideal balance between cost-effectiveness and service quality.
This   paper   addresses   this   challenge   by   examining   practical logistics network planning strategies tailored to SMEs. Using LPG BioMarkt GmbH—a regional organic food retailer in Berlin—as a case study, the research highlights how SMEs can employ   zone-based   clustering,   basic   planning   tools,   and collaborative   logistics   strategies   to   enhance   distribution performance. The findings offer a replicable model that other small-scale   manufacturers   can   adapt   to   their   own   regional distribution networks.  II.   Research Problem and Research Question  Despite being key contributors to regional economies, SMEs face major logistics challenges due to limited resources, small vehicle fleets, and high service expectations. Unlike large firms, they often lack access to advanced logistics planning software or third- party logistics partners. 1.   What   network   design   principles   are   applicable   for   SMEs serving regional markets? 2.   How can SMEs optimize their distribution points and routes without advanced software?  III.   Data Collection  The research relies on secondary data from academic journals, digital sources such as ScienceDirect and Statista, and company- specific   reports.   The   study   also   utilizes   internal   logistics flowcharts   and   observations   from   LPG   BioMarkt   GmbH’s operations.   These   sources   offered   both   quantitative   and qualitative   data,   providing   insight   into   the   challenges   and strategies relevant to SME logistics.
IV.   Research Overview  This study aims to:     Identify logistics challenges specific to SMEs     Analyze LPG BioMarkt’s logistics model     Develop   adaptable   strategies   for   similar   regional distributors Common SME logistics challenges include:     Limited budgets for logistics software     Inconsistent regional demand     Labor shortages and limited expertise     Difficulty balancing speed with cost The theoretical framework includes concepts from lean logistics, hub-and-spoke   distribution,   and   the   responsiveness-cost tradeoff. These models help understand how SMEs can simplify operations while maintaining service quality.  A.   Problem Identification  Scale Constraints:   Limited number of stores can drive high per-unit costs (transport, inventory). Network may be under- optimized.  Labor/Skills:   Like many EU SMEs, LPG faces workforce shortages and higher wage pressure (hard to hire skilled logistics staff)  Technology Gaps:   Absence of integrated WMS or route- optimization software means planning is manual and possibly inefficient.
Disruptions:   Global   events   (pandemics,   geopolitical) heighten risk for supply consistency, impacting inventory and delivery schedules.  V.   Data Analysis  A qualitative case study approach was used to analyze LPG BioMarkt’s logistics structure. The company operates 8 stores in the Berlin region, served by a central warehouse and outsourced 3PL delivery services. The delivery model follows a zone-based clustering strategy, manually optimized using Excel and Google Maps.  Key Findings from the Analysis:     Two-zone clustering reduced fuel costs by 12%     Delivery times stayed within an 18-hour target     Warehouse idle time decreased by 10% These   improvements   demonstrate   that   effective   logistics planning   does   not   necessarily   require   expensive   software. Instead, SMEs can leverage basic tools and strategic thinking to achieve measurable gains.  A. SWOT Analysis Strengths:   Strong   brand   identity   in   local   organic   market; sustainability   ethos   (products   within   200 km)   enhances reputationlpg-biomarkt.de; loyal customer base with membership discounts.  Weaknesses:   Small   scale   (less   economy   of   scale);   limited warehousing space; lack of advanced digital tools (ERP/WMS); labor-intensive operations.
Opportunities:   Growing   demand   for   organic/local   products; EU/regional support for local food networks; adoption of simple digital tools (e.g. route apps) to improve efficiency.  Threats:   Rising fuel and labor costs (compressing margins); competition from large organic chains (Alnatura, Dennree) with bigger   logistics   networks;   regulatory   changes   (e.g.   stricter organic labeling or emissions rules).  B. PESTEL Highlights Political:   EU/municipal initiatives often favor local agriculture and short supply chains.  Economic:   Inflation increases transport and labor costs (German inflation ~6% in 2024).  Social:   Consumers increasingly value sustainability and local sourcing (trends toward regional foods).  Technological:   LPG lags in tech; however, cloud-based WMS and free route-planning tools (Google Maps, OR-Tools) could be leveraged.  Environmental:   Local   sourcing   (200 km)   reduces   carbon footprint lpg-biomarkt.de, aligning with climate policies. Shift to electric delivery vehicles could further reduce impact.  Legal:   Strict organic certification and food safety laws must be met (impacting   supply choices). EU social regulations affect labor/transport compliance.
VI.   Findings  The   case   study   of   LPG   BioMarkt   GmbH   provides   valuable insights into how SMEs can balance cost and responsiveness in regional logistics. Through the implementation of a zone-based clustering model, the company achieved a 12% reduction in fuel costs and maintained delivery times within an 18-hour window, ensuring service reliability. Additionally, warehouse idle time was cut by 10%, indicating better operational coordination and labor efficiency. These outcomes highlight that even without advanced logistics systems, SMEs can achieve meaningful improvements by applying thoughtful strategies and leveraging accessible tools.  VII.   Conclusions  LPG BioMarkt demonstrates that SMEs can significantly improve logistics performance without high-tech solutions. By applying zone clustering and simple cost-benefit analysis tools like Excel, SMEs can reduce fuel consumption, enhance delivery speed, and reduce waste. These strategies not only address operational challenges but also contribute to environmental sustainability. The findings from this case study serve as a replicable framework for other small manufacturers and retailers facing similar logistical constraints.  VIII.   References  1.   Chopra, S., & Meindl, P. “CONTROLLING OF LOGISTICS BUSINESS PROCESSES: A CASE STUDY OF MAERSK”  Report By:  Prasanna Gaikwad 1   (241735) Omkar Kokate 2   (246426) Sanket Agalave 3   (242951) Guide- Dr. Behrooz Gharleghi  Department of Strategic Management in Logistics BBW Hochschule, Berlin, Germany  08 MAY, 2026
Abstract:  This paper examines the role of logistics management and strategic control in improving operational efficiency and competitive advantage in global supply chains, using A.P. Moller – Maersk as a case study. The study analyzes business processes in logistics management, benchmarking practices, and strategic planning techniques used by the company to manage complex international logistics operations.  The research highlights how Maersk integrates digital technologies, process automation, real-time tracking systems, predictive analytics, and sustainability initiatives into its logistics strategy. In addition, the paper evaluates Maersk’s logistics performance through benchmarking and performance management tools such as delivery reliability, supply chain visibility, and environmental sustainability metrics. The study also discusses major challenges affecting global logistics operations, including geopolitical conflicts,   supply   chain   disruptions,   fuel   price   volatility,   and   environmental   regulations.   Finally, recommendations are provided to improve strategic alignment through artificial intelligence, advanced analytics, green fuel investments, and enhanced supply chain resilience strategies. The findings demonstrate that integrated logistics planning, digital transformation, and sustainability-focused strategies are essential for maintaining long-term competitiveness in global logistics markets. Chapter 1. Business Process and its Role in Logistics Management – Case Study of Maersk 1.1 Introduction  A business process is a combination of certain steps carried out within an organization aimed at achieving the predetermined goal   (Amazon, 2024). A process in logistics management coordinates the transfer of products, information, and other resources through the supply chain. Efficient processes ensure logistics excellence and improve overall business performance. Maersk, as one of the leading global logistics service providers, operates an integrated system of logistics processes that include various aspects of transportation, warehousing, customs clearance, inventory movement, last-mile delivery services, among others. The company uses advanced logistics practices such as using digitalization, automation, and process optimization technologies   (A.P. Moller – Maersk, 2024).  1.2 Role of Business Process in Logistics Management  A business process plays a critical role in the field of logistics. The reason is that such process allows developing effective and consistent approaches for managing operations related to a supply chain, i.e., working with suppliers, ports, warehouses, freight carriers, and customers. In terms of business process management, this concept is crucial as it allows developing communication and operational management systems   (FedEx Corporation, 2024). Firstly, the business process is necessary to develop operational efficiency. Such an approach reduces the likelihood of errors, facilitates the use of resources, and optimizes operations (Heizer et al., 2020). For instance, logistics business processes such as automated tracking and management of goods within a warehouse enhance the efficiency of the operations. Secondly, the business process can be considered a technique that facilitates supply chain coordination, allowing partners to share data and collaborate in terms of logistics. Such cooperation can contribute significantly to enhancing inventory control, scheduling, and other aspects of logistics operation. Moreover, another function of the business process lies in increasing customer satisfaction through improved logistics processes. Modern requirements for delivering goods and shipment tracking have become increasingly stringent for logistics providers. Thus, process improvement should be prioritized. Lastly, the role of the business process is facilitating managerial decision-making by using performance indicators for monitoring logistics operation, e.g., on-time shipments, cost of transportation, and warehouse utilization rate(Christopher, 2022).
A. Process Techniques Applied by Maersk  Several techniques are currently being used in logistics processes at Maersk.  Process Standardization:  Maersk relies on standardization of logistics processes and practices in terms of shipping, clearing of cargo, and operations in logistics centers. Additionally, standardization allows for better coordination of work with international logistics partners. Digital Process Automation: The company has introduced numerous digital process management techniques in the form of: • Real-time cargo tracking • Automated booking systems • Route planning with AI • Predictive analytics for demand forecasting Such solutions allow enhancing operational performance, reducing the amount of manual work, and decreasing the risk of human error in logistics operations.  Lean Logistics and Optimization:  The company adheres to lean logistics principles, trying to optimize shipping routes, reducing costs, s aving fuel and time in ports and logistic centers. Integrated Supply Chain Management: An end-to-end integrated logistics approach includes shipping, warehousing, inland transportation, and logistics.  1.3 Challenges in Global Logistics Processes  However, although advanced process management brings many benefits to the business, there are also various challenges associated with global logistics processes. Among these are disruptions in the international supply chain due to political tensions, pandemics, increased congestion of transport hubs, among other factors. This leads to a decrease in operational effectiveness. Another problem is associated with the high cost of investments that should be directed to logistics processes improvement using modern digital tools and security systems. Moreover, management of global logistics processes is complicated by the need   to   consider local   regulations   in   different   countries   where global   operations   take   place. Cybersecurity threats pose significant problems due to reliance on logistics technologies.
1.4   Opportunities in Logistics Process Management  On the other hand, business process management provides numerous opportunities for logistics companies. For instance, the use of artificial intelligence technologies may facilitate better demand forecast and route optimization. Furthermore, tracking technologies provide greater supply chain visibility and contribute to improving customer satisfaction. Environmental sustainability is an important topic in logistics today, and Maersk invests in logistics sustainability through developing more fuel-efficient logistics operations and even building methanol-powered vessels. Finally, digital platforms are becoming an essential aspect of efficient logistics processes.
Chapter 2. Benchmarking and Performance Management in Logistics (MAERSK)  2. 1 Introduction  Benchmarking and performance management are essential tools for logistics companies operating in highly competitive global markets. Logistics firms use benchmarking to compare their operational performance, cost efficiency, service quality, and sustainability practices against industry leaders and competitors. Performance management helps organizations monitor key performance indicators (KPIs), improve operational efficiency, and achieve strategic goals (A.P. Moller – Maersk, 2024). A.P. Moller – Maersk (commonly known as Maersk) is one of the world’s largest integrated logistics and shipping companies. The company operates in more than 130 countries and manages ocean shipping, terminal operations, warehousing, inland transportation, and supply chain solutions. Due to increasing competition from companies such as DHL, MSC, FedEx, CMA CGM, and Hapag-Lloyd, Maersk continuously applies benchmarking and performance management techniques to maintain its competitive advantage (A.P. Moller – Maersk, 2024). This report analyzes the role of benchmarking in logistics management, evaluates Maersk’s logistics performance against industry benchmarks, and suggests improvements based on best practices from competitors.  2. 2   Benchmarking in Logistics Performance Measurement  A.   Definition of Benchmarking  Benchmarking is the process of comparing an organization’s operational performance, processes, and strategies with those of industry leaders or competitors to identify best practices and improve efficiency. In logistics management, benchmarking helps companies measure performance in areas such as:     Transportation cost efficiency     Delivery reliability     Supply chain visibility     Inventory management     Sustainability performance     Customer satisfaction
Benchmarking can be categorized into:     Internal Benchmarking:   Comparing performance across departments or branches within the same company.     Competitive Benchmarking:   Comparing performance with direct competitors.     Functional Benchmarking:   Comparing logistics processes with firms from different industries.     Strategic Benchmarking:   Evaluating long-term strategies and innovation practices. For Maersk, benchmarking is critical because the logistics and shipping industry faces increasing pressure regarding delivery speed, digitalization, sustainability, and operational costs (FedEx Corporation, 2024). Sustainability Improvement  Environmental benchmarking helps logistics firms reduce carbon emissions and improve energy efficiency. Digital Transformation  Benchmarking allows companies to evaluate digital capabilities such as real-time tracking, AI-based forecasting, and automation (DHL Group, 2024).

The study focuses on key logistics issues including delivery delays, food spoilage, inventory inefficiencies, and increasing sustainability pressures. To evaluate these challenges, the paper applies logistics management theories such as Lean Logistics, Just-in-Time (JIT), and Supply Chain Risk Management. In addition, the study analyzes the role of digital transformation technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI) and Internet of Things (IoT) systems, in improving logistics efficiency and operational performance. Strategic solutions such as AI-based demand forecasting, IoT-enabled cold-chain monitoring, and sustainable packaging initiatives are proposed to reduce waste, improve supply chain visibility, and strengthen sustainability performance. The study also highlights the importance of sustainable logistics practices in supporting United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production). Overall, the findings demonstrate that effective logistics control mechanisms and technological innovation are essential for improving operational efficiency and long-term sustainability within the global meal-kit industry.

Introduction  In today’s highly interconnected global economy, logistics and supply chain management play a critical role in ensuring operational efficiency, customer satisfaction, and business competitiveness. The rapid growth of e-commerce and online food delivery services has increased the importance of efficient logistics systems, particularly in industries dealing with perishable products and time- sensitive deliveries. Companies operating in the meal-kit delivery sector must manage complex supply chain networks while maintaining product freshness, reducing operational costs, and meeting increasing sustainability expectations (Christopher, 2023). HelloFresh is one of the world’s leading meal-kit delivery companies, operating across multiple international markets including Europe, North America, and Australia. The company delivers pre- portioned meal ingredients directly to customers through an extensive cold-chain logistics network. Due to the nature of its products, HelloFresh relies heavily on effective inventory management, temperature-controlled transportation, warehouse coordination, and last-mile delivery operations to maintain product quality and customer satisfaction (HelloFresh, 2024). However, managing cold-chain logistics presents significant operational challenges for HelloFresh. Issues such as food spoilage, delivery delays, fluctuating customer demand, and rising transportation costs can negatively impact operational performance and sustainability objectives. Additionally, increasing environmental concerns and pressure to reduce carbon emissions have forced logistics companies to adopt more sustainable and technologically advanced supply chain practices (Deloitte, 2024). This paper aims to analyze the cold-chain logistics and sustainability challenges faced by HelloFresh and evaluate the company’s logistics management processes using relevant supply chain and logistics theories. The study applies concepts such as Lean Logistics, Just-in-Time (JIT), and Supply Chain Risk Management to assess operational inefficiencies and identify improvement opportunities. Furthermore, the paper proposes strategic solutions involving digital transformation technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI), Internet of Things (IoT), and sustainable logistics practices to improve operational performance and long-term sustainability. The structure of this paper consists of an overview of HelloFresh’s logistics operations, an examination of its major logistical challenges, a theoretical analysis using logistics management frameworks,

7  Cold-chain logistics refers to the transportation and storage of temperature-sensitive products under controlled environmental conditions. In the case of HelloFresh, ingredients such as meat, dairy products, vegetables, and seafood require strict temperature management to avoid spoilage and contamination. This can lead to damaged products, customer complaints, and increased operational costs due to replacements and refunds. Another major challenge involves demand forecasting and inventory management. HelloFresh operates under a subscription-based business model where customer demand can fluctuate depending on seasonal trends, promotions, and changing consumer preferences. Inaccurate demand forecasting may result in either overstocking or understocking of fresh ingredients. Overstocking increases food waste and storage costs, while understocking can cause supply shortages and delayed customer deliveries. Managing inventory efficiently is therefore critical for maintaining operational stability and sustainability objectives. The company also faces growing pressure related to sustainability and environmental responsibility. Analysis Using Logistics Management Theories 4.1 Lean Logistics  Lean logistics focuses on minimizing waste, improving operational efficiency, and maximizing customer value throughout the supply chain process. The concept originates from lean management principles, where organizations aim to eliminate activities that do not create value for customers while
9  improving process efficiency and resource utilization (Christopher, 2023). In the logistics industry, lean practices are commonly used to reduce excess inventory, transportation inefficiencies, waiting times, and operational costs. For HelloFresh, lean logistics plays an important role in managing cold-chain operations and maintaining delivery efficiency. Since the company deals with highly perishable food products, reducing waste is essential for both profitability and sustainability. Excess inventory, inefficient transportation routes, and delayed deliveries can lead to food spoilage and increased operational expenses. Therefore, HelloFresh must continuously optimize its logistics processes to maintain efficiency across procurement, warehousing, packaging, and distribution activities.  Figure 4: Core Principles of Lean Logistics at HelloFresh  One example of lean logistics within HelloFresh’s operations is the use of demand-based inventory management. The company attempts to match ingredient procurement closely with customer orders to reduce unnecessary stock levels and minimize food waste. This approach helps lower storage costs while improving inventory turnover rates. In addition, route optimization technologies and centralized fulfillment   centers   support   lean   transportation   practices   by   reducing   delivery   times   and   fuel consumption. However, lean logistics also creates certain operational risks. Maintaining minimal inventory levels may   reduce   flexibility   during   unexpected   disruptions   such   as   supplier   delays,   transportation breakdowns, or sudden demand fluctuations. In practical terms, while lean systems improve efficiency, they may also increase supply chain vulnerability if contingency planning is insufficient.  4.2 Just-in-Time (JIT)  The Just-in-Time (JIT) approach is closely connected with lean logistics and focuses on receiving goods and materials only when they are needed in the production or delivery process. The primary objective of JIT is to reduce inventory holding costs and improve operational responsiveness. For food
10  delivery companies such as HelloFresh, JIT systems are particularly important because ingredients have limited shelf life and require rapid distribution to maintain freshness. HelloFresh’s subscription-based business model supports JIT operations because customer orders are collected before procurement and packaging activities begin. This allows the company to forecast ingredient requirements more accurately and reduce excess inventory. Fresh ingredients are sourced, packed, and delivered within short operational cycles, helping maintain product quality and reduce waste generation. The implementation of JIT provides several operational advantages. Firstly, it reduces warehousing requirements and storage expenses. Secondly, it improves inventory efficiency by minimizing overstocking and spoilage. Thirdly, customers benefit from fresher products and more responsive delivery systems. Any disruption within the supply chain can immediately affect operations because inventory buffers are limited.
